Estimate Inverse Probability Weights (Time Varying)

Source: R/ipwtm.R
ipwtm.Rd

Estimates inverse probability weights to fit marginal structural models with time-varying exposures and time-varying confounders across follow-up intervals. Supports binomial, survival, multinomial, ordinal, and gaussian families.

Usage

ipwtm(
  exposure,
  family = c("binomial", "survival", "multinomial", "ordinal", "gaussian"),
  link = NULL,
  numerator = NULL,
  denominator,
  id,
  tstart,
  timevar,
  type = c("first", "cens", "all"),
  data,
  corstr = "ar1",
  trunc = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

exposure

Name of the exposure column in data (unquoted or as a string).

family

Model family: "binomial", "survival", "multinomial", "ordinal", or "gaussian".

link

Link function for binomial or ordinal models.

numerator

Formula for numerator model. If NULL, unstabilized weights are computed.

denominator

Formula for denominator model. For family = "binomial", smooth terms (s(), te(), ti(), t2()) are allowed; the model is then fitted with mgcv::gam.

id

Name of the subject identifier column in data.

tstart

Name of the interval start time column (required for family = "survival").

timevar

Name of the follow-up (interval end) time column.

type

Exposure switch type: "first", "cens", or "all". "all" is available for all families. With family = "survival" and type = "all", exposure is an event indicator (1 when an exposure event, such as starting treatment, happens at the end of the interval) that may occur more than once per subject: an Andersen-Gill Cox model is fitted on all rows and every row contributes to the weights (Graffeo et al. 2018). For treatment that is started and stopped, compute weights separately for starting (on the rows off treatment) and for stopping (on the rows on treatment).

data

Data frame containing all required variables.

corstr

Correlation structure for GEE when family = "gaussian" (default: "ar1").

trunc

Optional truncation percentile between 0 and 0.5.

...

Additional arguments passed to model fitting engines.

Value

A list of class "ipwtm" containing:

ipw.weights

Numeric vector of inverse probability weights in original row order.

weights.trunc

Numeric vector of truncated weights (if trunc is specified).

call

Original function call.

selvar

Selection indicator vector (1 = active observation, 0 = post-switch).

num.mod

Numerator model object.

den.mod

Denominator model object.

Details

Standard errors: ipwtm only estimates the weights. Standard errors for the marginal structural model have to be obtained when that model is fitted. Robust standard errors, for example from coxph() with cluster(id) as in Van der Wal and Geskus (2011), treat the weights as known and tend to be conservative (too large). Austin (2016) compared naive, robust and bootstrap standard errors in simulations and recommends the bootstrap, in which the weights are re-estimated in each bootstrap sample. Austin studied a point treatment with baseline confounders; for longitudinal data in long format the bootstrap must resample subjects, not rows: keep all rows of a sampled subject, give each sampled copy a new id, re-run ipwtm (for treatment and, if used, censoring weights) on the bootstrap sample and refit the marginal structural model. See the cluster bootstrap in Example 1 below; ipwboot does this resampling for you (argument id). About 200 bootstrap samples are usually enough to estimate a standard error. Time-varying weights are products over time, so a few subjects can get very large weights. In the package's simulation study (500 subjects, 4 visits), bootstrap and robust standard errors were then both too small, with 95% confidence intervals covering the truth in only about 80% of samples. Check the weights with summary() and ipwplot, consider truncation (trunc), and interpret standard errors with care when the weights are extreme.

References

Graffeo N., Latouche A., Geskus R.B. & Chevret S. (2018). Modeling time-varying exposure using inverse probability of treatment weights. Biometrical Journal, 60(2), 323-332. doi:10.1002/bimj.201600223 .

Van der Wal W.M. & Geskus R.B. (2011). ipw: An R Package for Inverse Probability Weighting. Journal of Statistical Software, 43(13), 1-23. doi:10.18637/jss.v043.i13 .

Austin, P.C. (2016). Variance estimation when using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) with survival analysis. Statistics in Medicine, 35, 5642-5655. doi:10.1002/sim.7084 .

Examples

########################################################################
#EXAMPLE 1

#Load longitudinal data from HIV positive individuals.
data(haartdat)

#CD4 is confounder for the effect of initiation of HAART therapy on mortality.
#Estimate inverse probability weights to correct for confounding.
#Exposure allocation model is Cox proportional hazards model.
temp <- ipwtm(
  exposure = haartind,
  family = "survival",
  numerator = ~ sex + age,
  denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
  id = patient,
  tstart = tstart,
  timevar = fuptime,
  type = "first",
  data = haartdat)

#plot inverse probability weights
graphics.off()
ipwplot(weights = temp$ipw.weights, timevar = haartdat$fuptime,
        binwidth = 100, ylim = c(-1.5, 1.5), main = "Stabilized inverse probability weights")

#CD4 count has an effect both on dropout and mortality, which causes informative censoring.
#Use inverse probability of censoring weighting to correct for effect of CD4 on dropout.
#Use Cox proportional hazards model for dropout.
temp2 <- ipwtm(
  exposure = dropout,
  family = "survival",
  numerator = ~ sex + age,
  denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
  id = patient,
  tstart = tstart,
  timevar = fuptime,
  type = "cens",
  data = haartdat)

#plot inverse probability of censoring weights
graphics.off()
ipwplot(weights = temp2$ipw.weights, timevar = haartdat$fuptime,
        binwidth = 100, ylim = c(-1.5, 1.5),
        main = "Stabilized inverse probability of censoring weights")

#MSM for the causal effect of initiation of HAART on mortality.
#Corrected both for confounding and informative censoring.
#With robust standard error obtained using cluster().
require(survival)
summary(coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind + cluster(patient),
              data = haartdat, weights = temp$ipw.weights*temp2$ipw.weights))
#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind, data = haartdat, 
#>     weights = temp$ipw.weights * temp2$ipw.weights, cluster = patient)
#> 
#>   n= 19175, number of events= 31 
#> 
#>             coef exp(coef) se(coef) robust se      z Pr(>|z|)  
#> haartind -0.9363    0.3921   0.4299    0.4527 -2.068   0.0386 *
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#>          exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> haartind    0.3921      2.551    0.1614    0.9521
#> 
#> Concordance= 0.597  (se = 0.029 )
#> Likelihood ratio test= 5.57  on 1 df,   p=0.02
#> Wald test            = 4.28  on 1 df,   p=0.04
#> Score (logrank) test = 5.07  on 1 df,   p=0.02,   Robust = 4.83  p=0.03
#> 
#>   (Note: the likelihood ratio and score tests assume independence of
#>      observations within a cluster, the Wald and robust score tests do not).

#uncorrected model
summary(coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind, data = haartdat))
#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind, data = haartdat)
#> 
#>   n= 19175, number of events= 31 
#> 
#>             coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)
#> haartind -0.5862    0.5565   0.4368 -1.342     0.18
#> 
#>          exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> haartind    0.5565      1.797    0.2364      1.31
#> 
#> Concordance= 0.569  (se = 0.032 )
#> Likelihood ratio test= 1.97  on 1 df,   p=0.2
#> Wald test            = 1.8  on 1 df,   p=0.2
#> Score (logrank) test = 1.85  on 1 df,   p=0.2
#> 

#Bootstrap standard error for the MSM above (cluster bootstrap by patient).
#cluster() gives a robust standard error that treats the weights as known and
#tends to be conservative. Austin (2016) recommends the bootstrap, with the
#weights re-estimated in each bootstrap sample.
#With longitudinal data, resample patients, not rows: keep all rows of a
#sampled patient, give each sampled copy a new id, re-run both ipwtm() calls
#and refit the MSM.
#B = 20 keeps the example short; use about 200 in practice.
# \donttest{
msm.fun <- function(d) {
  tw <- ipwtm(exposure = haartind, family = "survival",
              numerator = ~ sex + age, denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
              id = patient, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
              type = "first", data = d)
  cw <- ipwtm(exposure = dropout, family = "survival",
              numerator = ~ sex + age, denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
              id = patient, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
              type = "cens", data = d)
  d$w <- tw$ipw.weights * cw$ipw.weights
  coef(coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind, data = d,
             weights = w))["haartind"]
}
rows.pat <- split(seq_len(nrow(haartdat)), haartdat$patient)
set.seed(123)
B <- 20
est.boot <- numeric(B)
for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  pick <- sample(length(rows.pat), replace = TRUE)
  d.boot <- haartdat[unlist(rows.pat[pick]), ]
  d.boot$patient <- rep(seq_along(pick), lengths(rows.pat[pick]))
  est.boot[b] <- msm.fun(d.boot)
}
#log hazard ratio with bootstrap standard error
c(estimate = unname(msm.fun(haartdat)), boot.se = sd(est.boot))
#>   estimate    boot.se 
#> -0.9363330  0.5091285 
#percentile interval (crude with B = 20)
quantile(est.boot, c(0.025, 0.975))
#>       2.5%      97.5% 
#> -2.0041188 -0.3006563 
# }

########################################################################
#EXAMPLE 2

data(basdat)
data(timedat)

#Aim: to model the causal effect of active tuberculosis (TB) on mortality.
#Longitudinal CD4 is a confounder as well as intermediate for the effect of TB.

#process original measurements
#check for ties (not allowed)
table(duplicated(timedat[,c("id", "fuptime")]))
#> 
#> FALSE 
#>  6291 
#take square root of CD4 because of skewness
timedat$cd4.sqrt <- sqrt(timedat$cd4count)
#add TB time to dataframe
timedat <- merge(timedat, basdat[,c("id", "Ttb")], by = "id", all.x = TRUE)
#compute TB status
timedat$tb.lag <- ifelse(with(timedat, !is.na(Ttb) & fuptime > Ttb), 1, 0)
#longitudinal CD4-model
require(nlme)
#> Loading required package: nlme
cd4.lme <- lme(cd4.sqrt ~ fuptime + tb.lag, random = ~ fuptime | id,
               data = timedat)

#build new dataset:
#rows corresponding to TB-status switches, and individual end times
times <- sort(unique(c(basdat$Ttb, basdat$Tend)))
startstop <- data.frame(
  id = rep(basdat$id, each = length(times)),
  fuptime = rep(times, nrow(basdat)))
#add baseline data to dataframe
startstop <- merge(startstop, basdat, by = "id", all.x = TRUE)
#limit individual follow-up using Tend
startstop <- startstop[with(startstop, fuptime <= Tend),]
startstop$tstart <- tstartfun(id, fuptime, startstop) #compute tstart (?tstartfun)
#indicate TB status
startstop$tb <- ifelse(with(startstop, !is.na(Ttb) & fuptime >= Ttb), 1, 0)
#indicate TB status at previous time point
startstop$tb.lag <- ifelse(with(startstop, !is.na(Ttb) & fuptime > Ttb), 1, 0)
#indicate death
startstop$event <- ifelse(with(startstop, !is.na(Tdeath) & fuptime >= Tdeath),
                          1, 0)
#impute CD4, based on TB status at previous time point.
startstop$cd4.sqrt <- predict(cd4.lme,
                              newdata = data.frame(id = startstop$id,
                                                   fuptime = startstop$fuptime,
                                                   tb.lag = startstop$tb.lag))
#compute inverse probability weights
temp <- ipwtm(
  exposure = tb,
  family = "survival",
  numerator = ~ 1,
  denominator = ~ cd4.sqrt,
  id = id,
  tstart = tstart,
  timevar = fuptime,
  type = "first",
  data = startstop)
summary(temp$ipw.weights)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.2117  0.9409  0.9908  1.0373  1.0125 13.6539 
ipwplot(weights = temp$ipw.weights, timevar = startstop$fuptime, binwidth = 100)

#models
#IPW-fitted MSM, using cluster() to obtain robust standard error estimate
require(survival)
summary(coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ tb + cluster(id),
              data = startstop, weights = temp$ipw.weights))
#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ tb, data = startstop, 
#>     weights = temp$ipw.weights, cluster = id)
#> 
#>   n= 84494, number of events= 134 
#> 
#>      coef exp(coef) se(coef) robust se     z Pr(>|z|)   
#> tb 0.8127    2.2541   0.1901    0.2599 3.127  0.00177 **
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#>    exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> tb     2.254     0.4436     1.354     3.751
#> 
#> Concordance= 0.57  (se = 0.024 )
#> Likelihood ratio test= 17.4  on 1 df,   p=3e-05
#> Wald test            = 9.78  on 1 df,   p=0.002
#> Score (logrank) test = 19.09  on 1 df,   p=1e-05,   Robust = 8.46  p=0.004
#> 
#>   (Note: the likelihood ratio and score tests assume independence of
#>      observations within a cluster, the Wald and robust score tests do not).
#unadjusted
summary(coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ tb, data = startstop))
#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ tb, data = startstop)
#> 
#>   n= 84494, number of events= 134 
#> 
#>      coef exp(coef) se(coef)     z Pr(>|z|)    
#> tb 1.4954    4.4612   0.1811 8.257   <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#>    exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> tb     4.461     0.2242     3.128     6.362
#> 
#> Concordance= 0.636  (se = 0.024 )
#> Likelihood ratio test= 63.84  on 1 df,   p=1e-15
#> Wald test            = 68.17  on 1 df,   p=<2e-16
#> Score (logrank) test = 79.8  on 1 df,   p=<2e-16
#> 
#adjusted using conditioning: part of the effect of TB is adjusted away
summary(coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ tb + cd4.sqrt, data = startstop))
#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ tb + cd4.sqrt, 
#>     data = startstop)
#> 
#>   n= 84494, number of events= 134 
#> 
#>              coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)    
#> tb        0.24618   1.27913  0.24288  1.014    0.311    
#> cd4.sqrt -0.24444   0.78314  0.03313 -7.378 1.61e-13 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#>          exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> tb          1.2791     0.7818    0.7947    2.0590
#> cd4.sqrt    0.7831     1.2769    0.7339    0.8357
#> 
#> Concordance= 0.738  (se = 0.025 )
#> Likelihood ratio test= 124  on 2 df,   p=<2e-16
#> Wald test            = 118.9  on 2 df,   p=<2e-16
#> Score (logrank) test = 136.6  on 2 df,   p=<2e-16
#>
